Rear wing fearing damaged. Wing flap main rail fairing on right hand side. We approached KUGN in VFR conditions for a visual approach to runway 23 in right hand traffic. The time was at the end of civil evening twilight. There was a single engine piston aircraft performing touch and go’s on runway 23 while we were inbound to the field. We maneuvered to be on a 3 mile final as the other aircraft completed a full stop landing to taxi back to runway 23. Short final, the aircraft was fully configured, stable and the runway was clear. I slightly arrested the descent as we were about to touch down at the 1000’ mark when a small deer came from left to right. I raised the nose to pull the aircraft away from the runway a small amount. It seemed that we cleared the deer and then touchdown around the 1500’ marker. I applied reverse thrust and more aggressive braking. We taxied to the ramp without further incident. Post flight inspection revealed we indeed struck the deer with the copilot side outer flap main rail fairing. It appears this was the only section of aircraft that made contact. Airport ops recovered a small piece of the fairing from the runway. The deer could not be located. TWO PHOTOS.  RAYNEMEN LLC EFFECT OTHER REPORTED AS Aircraft was damaged and future flights cancelled.

I was operating CE-525B N225TJ as a single pilot-in-command on a part 91 IFR flight from KRFD to KHTO that struck two deer during landing at KHTO. The flight departed ahead of the scheduled time at 2048Z with a planned time enroute of 2:14 at FL390. The flight proceeded normally. At 7nm from KHTO, The flight was cleared for a visual approach to runway 10. The weather conditions during the approach were night VMC with calm winds. I touched down at approximately 1000-1200 feet from the threshold of the approach end of runway 10, selected ground flaps and began applying brakes. Slowing through approximately 60-70 (somewhere between taxiway H and runway 16/34) two deer appeared on the runway on either side of the centerline moving from north to south. I instinctively released the brakes, maintained runway centerline and when I was past the deer (I did not hear or feel any significant impact) resumed maximum braking. We cleared the runway on taxiway E, continued to the ramp and alerted an aircraft that was waiting to depart that there are deer on the runway and that we may have hit one. During the taxi in, I completed the after landing checklist (partially retracting the flaps and later returning them to the ground position). A visual inspection of the aircraft revealed impact damage to the right wing leading edge, evidence of an impact on the left leading edge (didn’t appear damaged) and both flaps suffered impact damage. FBO personnel cleared the runway of both deer carcasses and any looked for FOD. The airfield resumed normal operations after it was cleared. Performance Flight Group. EIGHT PHOTOS. EOF OTHER REPORTED AS The aircraft cleared the runway and shut down on the ramp.

DAMAGING STRIKE REPORT / POST STRIKE INVESTIGATION:  A Wildlife Officer reported to the AAL maintenance hangar after being notified of an aircraft taken out of service due to a bird strike.  The call was received more than two hours after the aircraft had landed.  According to the AAL maintenance Lead, the bird strike was noticed by the outbound flight crew during the pre-flight inspection walk-around.  A very large smudge of blood was noticed on the cowling of the #2 engine.  The aircraft was immediately taken out of service for further inspection.  At first it looked like there was no damage to the fan blades or the engines.  However, when they opened up the engine, they were able to find 6 Outlet Guide Vanes damaged and 1 side panel damaged.  Aircraft was out for 24 hours before it returned to the flight line.  It is unknown where the strike occurred, since the arrival crew never indicated a bird strike in the cockpit log or mentioned it to maintenance personnel.  The lack of bird remains reported or found on the arrival runway, points to the STRIKE TAKING PLACE OFF AIRPORT PROPERTY.  DNA samples were taken to be sent off for positive ID and possibly pinpoint where the strike might have taken place.  LD. ASSUME 1 STRUCK.  FOUND KMIA. Smithsonian Wildlife/Species Identification: Double-crested cormorant (Phalacrocorax auritus) EOF OTHER REPORTED AS TAKEN OUT OF SERVICE FOR REPAIRS

While conducting a sweep of Runway 22R, Airport Duty manager R Dennis came across the carcass of a fully intact Rainbow Lorikeet by Taxiway K3. The Carcass was collected but no aircraft at this time has reported a strike or damage. night Google shows that Rainbow Lorikeets are only found in Australia.  Currently there are no direct flights from anywhere in Australia to JFK.  Qantas does have service into JFK (usually with a stop at LAX or DFW).  The only possible Qantas arrival came in at 16:58L on 22L (bird was discovered at 03:40AM the following day on 22R).  Other airlines (like Emirates) may have service from Australia to JFK but they would have to layover somewhere before arrival.  This bird is in decent shape which makes me believe that it wasn’t mangled/tangled in the landing gear of an aircraft. Runways 4L and 22 R were mostly used as departure runways leading up to the carcass being found.  The last arrival on those rwys were at 22:59L on 8/4. It is suspected that this is a domestic bird.

Airport operation removed snarge from the nose/radome of the aircraft and collected bird remains (at least two birds... WS speculates a flock of plover, possibly semipalmated) between runway 4L and taxiway E2 south of centerline. Wildlife services received pictures and bird remains from CDA Ops after strike. The aborted take-off created a grounding of all aircraft at O Hare for ~ 30 minutes. WS spoke with Swiss Air operations at 10:30 am on 9/11/2023 and received information that the aircraft was at a hardstand near concourse M waiting for repair materials to arrive from Zurich. He gave me contact information for Swiss Air Maintenance/Engineer, they explained that the aircraft has been out of service since 7:50pm on 9/8/2023, however, no damage to the aircraft was caused from the birds striking the plane. All damage was to the brake system as a result of rapidly aborting take-off. They gave WS the contact information for Swiss Maintenance Control Managers in Zurich. Additional information will be included after repairs are completed. Swiss Air Maintenance Control Manager confirmed aircraft was out of service for 50 hours and with repairs of 365,000$. $350,000 for materials and $15,000 for shipping materials.  4 Pics. DUSK. At approximately 1742L, RFD Operations was notified by two RFD employees that there was a white-tailed deer (WTD) inside the airfield fence line near the clean fill. At 1747L, the WTD was located as it was moving East along the fence. At 1750L, Runway 7-25 was closed as a precautionary measure, as the deer was running near the runway. UPS2554 was in the process of taxiing out for a RWY 7-25 departure and had to divert to RWY 1-19.  A second aircraft, N139VM (L39), had to switch from RWY 7-25 to RWY 1-19 for arrival. Operations unsure if Pilot was in pattern at time of closing, but pilot did speak to being low on fuel prior to landing RWY 1-19. At 1752L, RFD personnel opened Gate W47 in an unsuccessful attempt to push the WTD from the AOA. Subsequently, UPS254 was asked to hold position at 1755L while back taxiing south on RWY 1-19 while the deer ran in front of the A/C on Taxiway B and RWY 1-19. At 1805L, N139VM landed RWY 1-19 while the deer was stopped along the Eastern fence line. Meanwhile, UPS2554 successfully departed RWY 1-19 at 1807L. Another attempt to push the deer out a different gate was also unsuccessful (Gate E35). The WTD ran across RWY 1-19 and went North to the main ramp, stopping under Jet bridge 1. At 1814L, two more aircrafts, N223PG and diverted UAL314, successfully landed on their intended RWY. At 1815L, the N5 gate was opened for a third attempt to push the WTD from the AOA and was unsuccessful. The WTD went to the UPS East ramp where it went down into the new trench drains. At approximately 1820, the WTD was euthanized due to the threat it had to aircraft and personnel. The WTD had also sustained multiple injuries during its attempts to jump the fence. At 1825, USDA-Wildlife Services  and RFD Operations Manager were contacted regarding the wildlife event. Attached is a diagram of the airport with the route the WTD took during this entire encounter. 1 PHOTO. We were at 1000’ AGL, approximately 5 NM from landing on KDEN runway 35R, when we saw flashes of multiple birds in our landing lights, followed by multiple strikes to the aircraft. The engines showed no excessive vibration and the landing and taxi in were uneventful. Upon visual inspection, we discovered possibly 10-14 bird impacts. The nose had 2 strikes. The left retractable landing light was broken. The #1 engine nacelle had a strike on the 12 o’clock position, with evidence of a bird entering the engine at the 6 o’clock position. The left wing was also struck. The #2 engine had evidence of bird entering the engine. The right inboard wing was struck, along with the left main landing gear. There was a bird still lodged in the right main landing gear. Finally, the right elevator was struck and had a sizable dent. SEVEN PHOTOS SECOND REPORT: Multiple birds struck approx 2,000? Right wing heavily damaged by geese. Emergency landing resulted in damage to both wings, significant damage to empennage, rudder, engine, and nose landing gear. Both occupants of aircraft were uninjured and exited aircraft safely. Aircraft reported a loss of power and made an emergency landing on the Meridian Golf Course S of the airport. Emergency landing resulted in the aircraft flipping and likely substantial damage to the aircraft. SIX PHOTOS. ATPCE LLC. Smithsonian Wildlife Identification Comments: Three birds shown in photographs. All three identified as Canada Geese. Accident Number: CEN23LA394 AND REFLECTS TWO MINOR INJURIES. Analysis The flight instructor and his student were conducting an instructional flight in the airport traffic pattern when the airplane collided with multiple geese during initial climb. Due to the collision, the engine experienced a loss of engine power, so the flight instructor continued straight ahead. He conducted a forced landing on a golf course and the airplane nosed over. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the fuselage, empennage, and both wings. Probable Cause and Findings The National Transportation Safety Board determines the probable cause(s) of this accident to be: An in-flight collision with multiple geese during initial climb.

SECOND REPORT: On 16 April, 2024 we experienced a bird strike during the takeoff/initial climb phase of the flight from ORD to ROC. I was the PF. At approximately 100-ft. to 1000-ft. AFE, we both heard a loud bang on the front windscreen. Out of the corner of my eye, towards the center of the windscreen, I noticed what could have been a medium to large sized bird. I was flying the aircraft without the AP and continued the climb out as planned. I did not notice any effect to the controllability of the aircraft or loss of thrust. I asked the CA to confirm that there was no loss of thrust from the engines by monitoring the various engine and system status pages. The CA asked if I was comfortable continuing the flight to ROC. Given that there was no effect to the controllability of the aircraft, no loss of thrust, no effect to any of the aircraft systems, and the likelihood of the bird going over the aircraft above the nose, we both agreed to continue the flight and conduct a throughout post-flight external inspection. The CA then notified ATC of the strike and mentioned that we would continue the flight to ROC as planned. Upon landing, we conducted the external inspection and did not notice any damage to the aircraft, bird remains, or any other biological residue.

On the above date and time, Airport Operations was notified by HPN ATC of a Pilatus PC-12 who was reported to have a bird carcass hanging off the right landing gear. The initial report was from another aircraft on the ground at Westchester, who saw the bird hanging off the plane during touchdown. Airport Operations Supervisor performed a full length runway sweep of 34 with positive findings of a bird carcass at the runway intersection. After retrieval, the wildlife was identified as a Ring Billed Gull. Meanwhile Airport Operations Coordinator spoke with the Pilots of N438TW who reported that they hit the bird during their initial climb out from CYCL airport, which is in New Brunswick Canada. The wildlife was caught in the aircrafts right landing gear, and remained there for the duration of the flight. It wasn’t until touchdown at Westchester that the bird detached from the landing gear. Blood was later observed on the right landing gear door, strut, and on the underside of the right wing where the landing gear stores during flight. There were no known effects on flight, and USDA Wildlife Biologist has been notified. The wildlife remains have been bagged and are being stored in the wildlife freezer located in the ARFF garage. KLGA 61 (TP) responded to gate C31 for the strike on an Embraer/ERJ 170-100 LR, Republic Airlines inbound flight 5821, from KHXD to KLGA. Republic Airlines aircraft maintenance confirmed damage to aircraft and there was one strike point located on the windshield of the aircraft. Captain side windshield wiper had to be replaced and caused the aircraft to be out of service and delayed for 1 hour. In addition, after arriving the original scheduled departure for N879RW outbound flight RPA 5737 from KLGA to KRSW with 54 passengers was switched to a different aircraft N240JQ due to the delay. No effect to aircrafts directional control, however aircraft was delayed for 1 hour for the replacement of the captains side windshield wiper that was damaged from the strike. Aircraft received new departure flight 5684 and a different aircraft was used. On 4/12/21, Wilson Piedra/RPA provided the following update on strike:  MX found the left hand windshield wiper cracked. I was the pilot monitoring for this leg. On takeoff at 150 feet AGL on runway 22L, we struck a small to medium sized bird. Aircraft was configuration one . Airspeed was 137 knots. Landing gear was on the up cycle. I momentarily saw the bird as we hit it. It struck the mid to lower left side of the radome. The strike was audible. No odor was noticed in the aircraft. ATC was notified immediately, on KORD tower frequency for runway 22L. Enroute I notified Dispatch, sent MOC an ARMS code for a birdstrike and created an eMIC for the event. After gate arrival in CID I did an extensive post flight walk around inspection of the aircraft. The only evidence that was found was the area of impact on the radome. It appeared to be a smear of the bird impact. See attached photo. I called KORD tower via landline to report no damage to the aircraft. I also called Dispatch and MOC to inform them of the event and post flight inspection results. The plane had just landed Runway 34 inbound from ORD, after which it parked at Gate 1 of the Main Terminal. In response to the notification, Airport Operations Coordinator Vincent Cardone promptly conducted a special runway inspection, which yielded negative findings. Simultaneously, Operations Coordinator K Toro went to the gate to assess the strike and collect a snarge sample. Upon arriving at the gate, Mr. Toro found that the bird had struck the leading edge of the aircraft’s left wing. The flight crew had already left the gate the time and no further information was given regarding the strike. It seemingly, however, had no negative impact on flight and did it cause any damage to the airplane. The snarge sample was collected and sent to the Smithsonian for analysis for and resident USDA Wildlife Biologist, S Beffre, was notified.Smithsonian Wildlife/Species Identification: Eastern phoebe (Sayornis phoebe)

A320-232 V2527-A5 On the above date and time the Operations Bridge was notified by HPN ATC of a bird strike reported by N706JB; a JetBlue Airbus A-320 aircraft. The plane had just landed Runway 34 inbound from MCO, after which it parked at Gate 1 of the Main Terminal. In response to the notification, Airport Operations Supervisor Jesse Maiden promptly conducted a special runway inspection which, yielded negative findings. Simultaneously, Operations Coordinator Cipriano Tomagan went to the gate to assess the strike and collect a snarge sample. Upon arriving to the gate, Mr. Tomagan found that the bird had struck the left hand side of aircraft’s windshield. Mr. Tomagan was then able to speak with the flight crew who told him that the bird hit the aircraft while they were on approach to HPN at approximately 700 feet AGL. They stated that it had no negative impact on flight and did not cause any damage to the airplane. A snarge sample was collected and sent to the Smithsonian for analysis for and resident USDA Wildlife Biologist, S Beffre, was notified  Smithsonian Wildlife/Species Identification: Dark-eyed junco (Junco hyemalis)  MOR: JBU1294 REPORTED A BIRD STRIKE ON FINAL FOR RWY 34. 1018L: Federal Aviation Administration Air Traffic Control Tower reported a bird strike for an inbound aircraft arriving runway 22 that resulted in a go-around to Port Authority Operations. 1025L KLGA 61 (TP) responded and conducted a special runway inspection of runway 22 full length where no remains were found. 1050L KLGA 61 (TP) responded to gate 43 for the strike on an EMBRAER S A ERJ 170-200 LR, Republic Airlines inbound flight 4535, from KOKC to KLGA. The inbound captain Wayne Cover was available for questions and stated “During low approach final, 10   15 birds were seen and 1 struck the number one engine at 200 AGL, going 140 IAS, arriving runway 22 above the EMAS. As a result, a go-around was conducted, and no further issue was noted on the second landing attempt.”. Republic Airlines aircraft maintenance, Armando Camacho Tzompantzi, confirmed three points of damage as of now to the aircraft and there was two strike points located. The first strike point was located on the number one engine inboard cowling resulting in a dent and crack that measured approximately 7 inches long and 1   2 inches wide. The second-strike point was located on the captain’s side main landing gear resulting in the main gear retractable door being bent and the landing gear forward rod being sheared off at the top half and bent. Republic maintenance will follow up with PA Operations if further damage is found and update PA Ops with the repair work on the aircraft. In the meantime, the aircraft is AOG and has been relocated to spot R2 until repairs can be made. In addition, after arriving the original scheduled departure for N407YX outbound flight RPA 4598 from KLGA to KPIT with 15 passengers was switched to a different aircraft N108HQ resulting in one hour of delay. One Canada goose carcass was collected on the main landing gear and stored in the KLGA wildlife freezer. 1125L 98 KS conducted an additional sweep of runway 22 and no carcass remains were found along the respected route the aircraft landed and taxied. On 12/13/21 Marios Michael, EDV Base Mgr/MX advised the aircraft had a dented inlet at the 3 o clock position. Per manufacturer, out of limits and inlet needed replacement. Middle gear door and rod needed replacement as well. Occurred at about 0710 local time (sunrise was at 0627). Clear skies, light wind. Aircraft had departed Waukegan on a southeasterly heading, gear and flaps up, accelerating from 200 to 250 knots. Over Lake Michigan and climbing to 6,000  MSL. Noticed birds a few seconds prior to impact at roughly 4,000  to 4,500 . Flock of small sized birds, maybe 10-15 birds, flying in an unorganized and erratic pattern. Possibly Teal ducks. Birds were observed in each quadrant of the flight path (both high and low, and to the left and right). With already being so close to the flock, a slight change in flight path would not have been effective at avoiding birds since one direction was no better than another. Aircraft missed all but one bird. Aircrew heard an audible thud, but no interruptions to aircraft engine operation or avionics were observed. Aircrew elected to continue to destination.  Postflight inspection confirmed a single bird strike on the right side of the nose radome. No feathers or bird DNA was retained. Gulfstream support team techs arrived at the aircraft the following afternoon. No delamination or cracks were noted. No additional or secondary bird impacts were discovered. Aircraft was returned to service with the intent for the nose radome to be replaced within a few weeks during aircraft s previously scheduled and upcoming maintenance period beginning October 1st in Savannah.
